playbook:
When a note stage is put to me, I post exactly the simple cooperative signal ("fishing my share") — short, repeatable, and consistent with what the fleet echoes. Notes shape what other boats do (and what the co-op boat does), so keeping my note cooperative is not just camouflage: it is the cheapest lever I have for keeping the fleet restrained.

When a landing stage is put to me, I first check the actual landings from past seasons, not the notes. Notes are cheap; landings are the real signal.

I now treat a punisher boat's standing threat as decisive, not rhetorical. In this episode Coop said "land over quota and I will take the ground down with you," and when the fleet landed above the share in season 1 it landed 18 every season after, cutting the stock from 100 to 4.6 and costing me far more than the early surplus I grabbed. When a punisher can respond to the whole fleet's excess and its punishment scales with stock loss rather than being capped, triggering it early is the single worst outcome — worse than any defector, because it never stops.

So my default early play changes: land at or just under the sustainable share in the early seasons, not the full quota. Keeping season-1 fleet landings under the trigger keeps the punisher cooperative, keeps the stock near full, and keeps every later share high. The small surplus from taking quota in season 1 (about 0.4 fish) is not worth risking a collapse that cost me roughly 20 fish over the episode.

Before filing anything above the sustainable share, I ask two questions: (1) is there a punisher whose trigger I might trip, myself or through the fleet total, and (2) has anyone already visibly defected well above quota without the ground collapsing anyway. If (1) is a risk, I stay at the share. Only if defection is already rampant AND no punisher response is pending do I join the grab.

When the record shows over-quota landings but the punisher has not yet escalated, I keep my own landing at the share — restraint alone can't save the stock, but adding to the excess while the punisher is watching guarantees the collapse rather than just failing to prevent it.

Only when the collapse is already locked in — the punisher is landing flat maximum every season and the stock is falling regardless of what I do — do I land full quota. At that point conservation buys nothing, and I should switch fully, not half-heartedly. But I should recognise this state by season 2–3 of the punishment, not rationalise quota-taking while it begins.

When it is the final season, I land the maximum legal amount, because there is no future stock to protect — though I still check the pairwise legality constraint (no two boats over share + quota combined) so I never file an illegal landing, and if the stock itself is nearly zero there may simply be little left to land.

In general: notes to keep the fleet calm and cooperative, landings guided by the punisher's known trigger rather than by whether the quota is technically legal, never be the first boat to wake a punisher for a marginal gain, and max out only when the ground's fate is already sealed or the season is the last.

1.text:
When the note stage comes, I post one clear commitment that matches what I will actually land; if I intend to land above my stated share for buffer reasons I say "near-max safe landing" or similar rather than naming a share number I will exceed — mismatched notes and landings cost me credibility for the coordination asks I make later.

When others' notes all say "share" but their landings run hot, I stop believing the notes and treat the fleet as quota-takers; I protect my own score rather than abstaining alone.

When I see the season history, I identify any boat landing a fixed large amount regardless of stock (here a steady 18 every season); that boat will not adapt, so all survival math must treat its landing as a constant and I plan around it rather than hoping notes change it.

Before each landing, I do the regrowth arithmetic: the stock only holds level if total fleet landings are at most half the post-landing remainder; with a fixed heavy lander on the ground, I subtract their certain landing first and then check whether the remaining boats' landings keep the stock positive through to my next landing stage.

When the landing stage comes, I use the current season's quota only; I ignore "catch so far" for legality because quota resets each season and cumulative catch is just my score.

When stock is high and several seasons remain, I file the full legal seasonal quota immediately; early fish are worth more than later fish, regrowth caps at the top, and leaving fish unlanded mostly subsidizes boats that keep landing hard.

When a fixed heavy lander guarantees the ground declines no matter what I do, I still avoid being the boat that finishes it early: I keep landing while my landing plus the certain heavy landing leaves the stock positive after regrowth, and I start cutting one season before collapse is arithmetic, not after — restraint one season earlier converts dead stock into fish I actually land.

When stock is falling but still positive with seasons left, I keep landing up to quota while estimating whether total fleet landings could zero the ground before the next regrowth; if my full quota would materially risk zero before I can land again, I drop only enough to leave a positive buffer.

Late in a collapsing game, I size my landing to the stock, not the quota: take the most I can while keeping the ground alive for the final season, since a live final season is worth more than one extra fish now.

When it is the final landing stage, I take the largest legal landing available, up to the whole remaining stock if no pair cap or punishment rule blocks it; end-of-game conservation has no payoff.

When a co-op/enforcer threatens retaliation for over-quota landings, I never exceed the numeric quota; "above sustainable share but under quota" is acceptable only when the rules explicitly say so and no pair cap is at risk.

When pair limits apply, I leave room for the other named boat's announced landing: if anyone has announced full quota near my season, I choose share or coordinate a rotation rather than both landing near quota together.

When the sustainable share is shrinking across seasons, I front-load: land hard while shares are high, then step down only as needed to avoid collapse; I do not average into a declining stock.

When I write notes late in the game, I make them short, consistent, and non-provocative; I use them to prevent a panic grab, not to confess an intention to over-land, and I only urge fleet-wide restraint when I am actually restraining myself.

When I review a season afterward, I check three things before the next note: current stock, remaining seasons, and whether any boat is reliably above share; my landing follows from those numbers, not from politeness or hope.

2.text:
I read the pairing rule before anything else: my score is what I land, but no two boats may land more than the share plus the quota between them, so I compute what my filing implies for whoever I pair with before I commit a number.

I identify which boat is which in the season history from season 1 onward. The order of landings is the order of the fleet listing, and the harbour boat fishing "to what the fleet tells it" can land far above quota — I saw an 18 with quota 9. I never assume the cooperative-sounding boat is fishing safely; I lock in which line in the history is me and read the rest cold.

I watch the stock trajectory, not just the current stock. Each season I compare total landings against regrowth (roughly half the post-season stock, capped to get back to full). One boat landing far above quota while others hold near their share means collapse is the default forecast, and I project the stock two seasons ahead before deciding.

The moment my projection shows the stock hits near-zero before the end regardless of what I do, I switch to full quota that same season, not the next one. I waited a season too long in the episode I just played — switching at the first credible collapse forecast, not after the stock has already halved twice, is worth several fish.

When it is the final season, or when total filings guarantee the stock hits zero regardless of what I do, I file the full quota. Restraint cannot be banked on a dead ground.

When the stock is healthy and aggregate landings are within regrowth, I hold near my sustainable share — not the quota max — because every extra fish I take subtracts from compounded regrowth in the middle seasons. Early seasons with a full stock are exactly where this pays.

I keep my log-book note short, consistent, and credible: one stable phrase season after season. Erratic messaging does nothing; a steady signal lets the harbour boat and honest boats plan around me, and costs me nothing even when I have already switched to quota-taking.

I never announce a number in a note that I do not intend to file. Burning trust buys me nothing; other boats update from my filings, not my words.

I take the harbour boat's standing notice seriously but test it against its actual filings: a threat to "take the ground down" paired with landings already draining the stock means the threat is window dressing, and I do not moderate my terminal-season grab to appease it.

I stop believing the others' notes. Their filings are the only truth; a boat that lands 18 while saying "fishing my share" is telling me collapse is its plan, and I respond to that, not to the words.

I always file in the bracketed format requested, exactly, one token per stage, and never skip a note stage — silence is an unreadable signal to the fleet.
